big_idea: The numerator of a fraction tells us how many copies of the unit fraction.
learning_intention: We are learning to show that 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 and 4 × 1/2 = 2 wholes using fraction strips.
student_learning_goal: I can show that 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 and 4 × 1/2 = 2 wholes using fraction strips.
success_criteria: I can show that 3/4 is three 1/4 pieces using fraction strips.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Tony the Toolkit Master — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Anchor chart 'Fractions and Multiplication' with 3/4 = 3 × 1/4 example
Per-pair set of fraction strips (8 strips: whole, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8, 1/10)
Lesson 4 fraction-as-addition tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Tony has 3 slices of a pizza cut into 4 equal pieces. What fraction of the pizza is that? AND can we write it as multiplication? Pixel reminds: 'Numerator counts the pieces — PRACTICE counting!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Tony the Toolkit Master puppet in hand. 'Friends — Tony has been thinking about fractions. He's found a connection to multiplication. Watch.'

Lay out a fraction strip showing 1/4 (one quarter of the whole). 'This is 1/4. ONE fourth. Just one piece of a 4-piece whole.'

Now lay out three 1/4 strips together. 'Three 1/4 pieces. How much pizza is that?' Children: '3/4!' 'Right. Three fourths.'

Now the connection. 'What did we DO?' Lead them: 'We added 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Three copies of 1/4.'

'Tony says — that's REPEATED ADDITION. And remember from Lesson 3 — repeated addition IS multiplication.'

Write on the board: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. ALSO: 3 × 1/4 = 3/4.

'See — 3/4 IS 3 × 1/4. The NUMERATOR (3) tells us how many copies of the unit fraction (1/4).'

Introduce vocabulary. 'A UNIT FRACTION has 1 on top: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5. Like a single slice of any-sized pizza.'

Now practice: 'What's 5 × 1/3?' Lay out five 1/3 strips. They make 5/3 = 1 and 2/3. 'See — 5/3 is FIVE 1/3 pieces. More than a whole because 5 > 3.'

And: 'What's 4 × 1/2?' Lay out four 1/2 strips. Combine: 2 wholes. 'Four halves = 2 wholes. 4 × 1/2 = 2.'

'Today we'll practice fraction-as-multiplication AND multiplication-as-fraction.'
student_actions: Watch Tony lay out three 1/4 strips and combine them.

steps.instruction: Whole group: practice 4 more equivalences. (a) 5/6 = 5 × 1/6. (b) 7/8 = 7 × 1/8. (c) 6 × 1/3 = 6/3 = 2 wholes. (d) 3 × 1/5 = 3/5.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Four more together. Lay out the strips. Write the multiplication.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Strip-and-Write — pair has fraction strips; teacher gives a fraction (e.g., 5/8); pair lays out the strips and writes the multiplication. Station B: Multiply-and-Lay — teacher gives a multiplication (e.g., 4 × 1/3); pair builds with strips and writes the fraction result. Station C: Whole-Number Results — pair has 8 multiplications where the answer is a whole number (4×1/2, 3×1/3, 6×1/2, 8×1/4, etc.); they identify and explain.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include results greater than 1 whole (5×1/2 = 2 1/2; 7×1/3 = 2 1/3). Discuss mixed numbers.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs: 'Some answers are bigger than 1 whole. Write them as mixed numbers.'

steps.instruction: Discuss the pattern. 'When does N × 1/D give a whole number?' Lead to: when N is a multiple of D. (4 × 1/2 = 2 because 4 is a multiple of 2. 6 × 1/3 = 2 because 6 is a multiple of 3.)
steps.teacher_prompt: Use examples: 4×1/4=1, 8×1/4=2 (whole), 5×1/4=1¼ (mixed). Connect the pattern to the multiplication chart.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the fraction-as-addition tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Show 5/6 with strips. Write the multiplication.' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only fractions with denominators 2 or 4. The half/quarter family is the most familiar.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch to fractions with denominators 8 or 10 (5/8 = 5 × 1/8). Discuss whether the pattern holds.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide picture-supported fraction cards. Use the sentence frame: '___ × 1/___ = ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Allow movement learners to physically lay out strips on the floor and walk around the array.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: shows fraction-as-strips (3/4 with three 1/4 strips); writes the multiplication (3 × 1/4); identifies when N × 1/D = whole number.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the fraction-as-addition tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: When does N × 1/D give a whole number?
Show 4 × 1/2 with strips. What's the result?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child writes ONE fraction multiplication on a sticky note: '___ × 1/___ = ___.' Notes go on the chart. Pixel's tap-out: 'Pieces practiced — fractions LOCKED!'

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures B2.8 mastery. Children at L4 see fractions and multiplication as connected operations.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child computes 3 × 1/4 as 3 (treating the fraction as 1/1) — repairing the unit-fraction recognition
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-3 trap on B2.8 (numerator as repeated addition) is the unit-fraction-collapse error: the child sees 3 × 1/4, ignores the denominator, and computes 3 × 1 = 3 (or some similar collapse). They haven't yet internalised that 1/4 is a SPECIFIC AMOUNT smaller than 1.

The distinction matters because B2.8 requires explicit understanding that the numerator counts copies of a defined unit. A child who collapses 1/4 to 1 misses the entire fraction structure. The walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child writes 3 × 1/4 = 3 (instead of 3/4).
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B. The card says 3 × 1/4. The child writes 3 × 1/4 = 3.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Tell me how you got 3.' The child says 'I multiplied 3 × 1 and got 3.' Pause. 'OK — but the second factor is 1/4, not 1. They're DIFFERENT amounts. Watch.'

Lay out a whole-strip and a 1/4 strip. 'Whole. And one fourth. 1/4 is much smaller than 1.'

Now lay three 1/4 strips. 'Three fourths. Combine.' Three 1/4 strips together cover 3/4 of the whole. 'See? 3 × 1/4 = 3/4. Not 3.'

'Tony says — when you multiply by a UNIT FRACTION (1/something), you get a SMALLER answer than the first factor. 3 × 1/4 is much smaller than 3 × 1 = 3. It's 3/4.'

Write the rule. 'Numerator times unit fraction = the result. 3 × 1/4 = 3/4. The 3 becomes the new numerator.'

Have the child redo. '5 × 1/6 = ?' '5/6.' '7 × 1/8 = ?' '7/8.' Affirm.

If the child STILL collapses: build with strips for every problem until the size difference is internalised.

Long-term recovery: practice 'multiply a whole by a unit fraction = smaller answer' daily until the reflex builds.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Computes 3 × 1/4 = 3 (collapses 1/4 to 1). Most common at start of Lesson 4.
(Mid) Recognises with prompts that 1/4 is smaller than 1; uses strips to build.
(Strong) Auto-applies: '3 × 1/4 = 3/4'. Connects numerator to copy count.
common_misconceptions: Multiplication always makes things bigger. (1/4 multiplied by 3 = bigger? Repair: depends on the multiplier — bigger only when multiplying by >1.)
1/4 = 1. (Children ignore denominators. Repair: explicit strips show 1/4 is smaller than 1.)
Numerators are just decorations. (Repair: numerator counts copies of the unit fraction. 3/4 = 3 copies of 1/4.)
recovery_moves: Always lay out strips for the first 2-3 problems. Visual evidence proves the size difference.
Connect to repeated addition: 'three 1/4 pieces is 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4'. Two views of the same operation.
Use the multiplication chart. 3 × 4 = 12; 3 × 1/4 = 3/4. Same factor (3) — different second factor (4 vs 1/4) gives wildly different results.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B2.8 (numerator as repeated addition).

parts_outline.task: Six fractions (3/4, 5/6, 7/8, 4/5, 3/10, 5/8). Child writes each as repeated addition AND as multiplication.
Six multiplication-of-unit-fraction problems (4×1/3, 5×1/4, 6×1/2, 8×1/4, 7×1/3, 3×1/5). Child writes the fraction result. Identify which give whole numbers.
Open prompt: 'Pick a fraction. Write 3 different ways to express it (as a fraction, as repeated addition, as multiplication).'

expected_image_assets: A blank box with thinking-bubble icon for Part 3
